newsitem.title: FRANCE: Netanyahu says no deal ever on Jerusalem, Golan.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says no deal ever on Jerusalem, Golan.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fresh from signing a deal on a partial pull-out from Hebron, has said there will never be any negotiation on Israeli rule over Jerusalem and the Golan heights.
He told the French daily Le Figaro in an interview to be published on Saturday whose text was released on Friday that Jerusalem would remain Israel's capital "for eternity".
"There will never be a redeployment in Jerusalem," he said.
The hardline premier said Israel and Damascus were inching towards resuming peace talks, but he ruled out any negotiation on the Golan which Israel seized from Syria in 1967.
"We must keep the Golan for strategic, historical and economic reasons," he said, citing the need for the Jewish state to retain the northern hills' crucial water reserves.
He said Israel and Syria were in touch through the United States, but Damascus had yet to accept proposals for talks.

"We are moving slowly but surely towards resuming peace talks," he said, adding some people believed the Syrians may be waiting for the installation of President Bill Clinton for a second term. He is to be sworn in on Monday.

He said France, which has been seeking a higher profile in the peace process, and Europe could play a role in the Middle East because of their good relationship with Arab countries -- if they adopted a more balanced and moderate stand.
Netanyahu did not rule out establishment of a Palestinian state on the autonomous territories, but set limits because of strategic reasons and the problem of minorities.
"We can consider it...But we must first define the word 'state'," he said. "We need a new model which would grant autonomy in some fields and not in others."
He said a Palestinian state would control the airspace over Jewish settlements, could place guns on hills overlooking Tel Aviv and pump underground water.
He also feared the Arab minority in Israel could demand to be integrated into a Palestinian state.
"We face two great dangers: nuclear proliferation and self-determination for minorities...As for me, I am looking for an alternative between subjection and self-determination," he said.
Chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen, said on Friday he was convinced that Netanyahu would ultimately agree to a Palestinian state.
Netanyahu, who came to power in June on a platform opposed to swapping occupied Arab land for peace, denied the Hebron deal had betrayed his voters and said it was fair for both sides.
"Our objective is to maintain a Palestinian autonomy deprived of some prerogatives that may endanger our country... This is exactly what we are doing," he said.

He said the deal was "neither good nor bad, but necessary" and he was expecting Palestinians to abide by their commitments to amend their charter calling for the destruction of the Jewish state, dismantle terrorist organisations and seize weapons.
Netanyahu threw back at the Palestinians charges that he procrastinated on the long-awaited accord, saying they slowed down the process two months ago although 95 percent of the deal was ready.
"This explains the delay, which is not on our part," he said.
